## Welcome

How can we learn from data, express what remains uncertain, and make useful predictions? This course develops Bayesian inference, modeling, computation, and model criticism using Python. We will connect Bayesian, frequentist, and Fisherian perspectives, following Efron and Hastie's distinction, while making each method's assumptions and interpretation explicit.

The required textbook is Agresti et al., *Foundations of Bayesian Statistics for Data Scientists: With R and Python*. Gelman et al. (BDA), Reich–Ghosh, and Efron–Hastie are supporting references; see [Resources](pages/resources.qmd).

## Proposed Course Roadmap {#course-roadmap}

Begin with [Why Bayesian?](slides/00-why-bayesian.html), a short motivational introduction to the three inferential perspectives. Then follow Agresti's chapters in seven decks. The technical introduction in chapter 1—Bayes' rule, posterior summaries, decisions, and prediction—belongs in [Foundations](slides/01-bayesian-foundations.html), after the opening overview.

The plan combines Agresti's progression with the earlier syllabus's Bayesian foundations, multiparameter normal models, large-sample inference, hierarchical models, posterior computation, regression, and advanced applications.

### Fifteen teaching weeks

Teaching-week numbers below exclude Spring Break; the dated [Schedule](pages/schedule.qmd) counts calendar weeks, including the break. This is a proposed sequence, with no assessment dates assigned.

| Teaching week | Proposed focus |
|---:|:---|
| 1 | Why Bayesian?; begin Foundations |
| 2 | Finish Foundations: posterior inference, prediction, and interpretation |
| 3 | Proportions: priors, conjugacy, and posterior prediction |
| 4 | Finish Proportions; begin Means and Normal Models |
| 5 | Means, unknown variance, joint and marginal inference |
| 6 | Finish normal models and approximations; begin Linear Models |
| 7–8 | Linear Models: regression, matrix formulation, checking, and regularization |
| 9 | Finish Linear Models; begin GLMs and Hierarchies |
| 10–11 | GLMs, partial pooling, hyperpriors, and multilevel prediction |
| 12–13 | Posterior Computation: Monte Carlo, MCMC, samplers, and diagnostics |
| 14 | Finish computation; begin Model Choice |
| 15 | Model comparison, selected extensions, and integrative model critique |

### How the topics fit together

- **Foundations before automation:** exact binomial and normal examples make posterior reasoning visible before more complex software fits.
- **Hierarchies are core:** exchangeability, partial pooling, and multilevel models retain the older syllabus's emphasis, including selected starred sections of Agresti.
- **Theory supports interpretation:** joint and conditional distributions, large-sample behavior, and normal/Laplace approximations connect inference to its mathematical foundations.
- **Computation serves modeling:** a short sampler/diagnostics primer accompanies early software use; the later computation deck explains the algorithms and revisits those models.
- **Extensions are selective:** mixtures and fuller multivariate models supplement Agresti. Classification, missingness, networks, or a Gaussian-process illustration compete for the optional time rather than enlarging the course.

The [Agresti contents and preface](https://bayes4ds.rwth-aachen.de/pdf/Bayes4DS-Contents.pdf) guide the chapter sequence. Efron–Hastie's [*Computer Age Statistical Inference*](https://hastie.su.domains/CASI/), chapters 2–4, supplies the three-perspective framing.
